title: What are the common sharding strategies: hash-based (consistent hashing on shard key: even distribution, hard range queries), range-based (date/ID ranges: easy range scans, risk of hot partitions), directory-based (lookup table maps key→shard: flexible, single point of lookup): and how do you choose the shard key (high cardinality, even distribution, aligned with query patterns)?
shortTitle: Common sharding strategies and choosing a shard key
keyPoints: Hash-based sharding hashes the shard key for even distribution, but range queries must scatter-gather across every shard.
Range-based sharding assigns contiguous key ranges, making range scans efficient but risking hot partitions with monotonically increasing keys.
Directory-based sharding keeps a lookup table mapping each key to its shard, offering maximum flexibility at the cost of an extra lookup on every access.
Consistent hashing with virtual nodes limits data movement when adding or removing shards to roughly 1/N of the keys.
A good shard key has high cardinality, distributes evenly, and aligns with the dominant query pattern so most queries hit a single shard.
The shard key is very hard to change later, so query patterns must be modeled before choosing it.
Composite shard keys can address multiple access patterns when a single key is insufficient.

s1_definition.oneliner: Hash spreads evenly but kills range scans; range enables scans but risks hotspots; directory is flexible but adds a lookup: pick the shard key by cardinality, evenness, and query pattern.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Hash-based** – `shard = hash(key) % N` or consistent hashing. Even distribution, fast single-key lookups, but range queries scatter-gather across all shards.
- **Range-based** – Contiguous key ranges per shard (date blocks, ID ranges). Easy range scans, but monotonically increasing keys create a hot shard.
- **Directory-based** – A lookup table maps each key to its shard. Maximum flexibility and granular rebalancing, but an extra lookup on every access.
- **Shard key criteria** – High cardinality, even distribution, aligned with the dominant query pattern.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India has too many accounts for one database, so it spreads them across several. Hash-based is like assigning accounts to branches by a scrambling formula so every branch is equally full. Range-based is like branch A keeps accounts 1 to a million: easy to grab a range, but if all new accounts land in the last branch it gets overloaded. Directory-based is like a central register that says exactly which branch holds Rajesh's account: flexible but you always consult the register first.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│            Sharding Strategies Comparison                 │
├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                            │
│  Hash-based:                                              │
│  Key → hash() → shard                                    │
│  [Even] [Fast lookup] [Bad range queries]                 │
│                                                            │
│  Range-based:                                             │
│  Key range → shard                                        │
│  [Good range scans] [Hot last shard] [Easy to add]        │
│                                                            │
│  Directory-based:                                         │
│  Key → lookup table → shard                               │
│  [Flexible] [Granular rebalance] [Extra lookup]           │
│                                                            │
│  Shard Key Selection:                                     │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐          │
│  │ High cardinality (millions of values)       │          │
│  │ Even distribution (no hot spots)            │          │
│  │ Aligned with dominant query pattern         │          │
│  │ Very hard to change later!                  │          │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────┘          │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Sharding splits one logical dataset across many physical databases, and the three common strategies trade off differently. Hash-based sharding hashes the shard key, usually with consistent hashing, giving even distribution and fast single-key lookups, but range queries must scatter-gather across every shard. Range-based sharding assigns contiguous key ranges so range scans stay on a few shards, but monotonically increasing keys create a hot shard. Directory-based sharding keeps a lookup table for maximum flexibility at the cost of an extra lookup on every access.

Choosing the shard key is the most consequential decision because it is very hard to change later. A good shard key has high cardinality so data spreads out, distributes evenly to avoid hotspots, and aligns with the dominant query so most requests hit a single shard. When a single key does not satisfy multiple access patterns, a composite key can help.

At the National Bank of India, the overwhelming access pattern is lookup by account_id, so Pankaj shards by account_id using consistent hashing with virtual nodes, which spreads load evenly and keeps single-account reads on one shard. He avoids keys like branch_city that would skew badly, and plans resharding from day one.

Remember one sentence: hash spreads evenly but hurts range scans, range enables scans but risks hotspots, and directory is flexible but adds a lookup, so choose the shard key by cardinality, evenness, and query pattern.
